name: Probes, lifecycle & graceful shutdown
objective: CKAD › Application Design and Build + Observability. Drill EVERY pod-design corner harder than the exam: classic vs native sidecars, init ordering, all three probe types and handlers, lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown, full securityContext hardening, QoS classes, the Downward API, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: All three probe types, three handlers
questions.teach:
Three probe kinds: **livenessProbe** restarts a failing container, **readinessProbe** pulls it from Service endpoints, **startupProbe** gates the other two until a slow app is up. Any probe uses one of three handlers: `exec`, `httpGet`, or `tcpSocket`.

**Gotcha:** timing fields (`periodSeconds`, `initialDelaySeconds`, `failureThreshold`) attach per-probe — set each on the right probe.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `health-pod` in `pod-design` (`nginx:1.25`, one container `web`) with all three probes:
- **livenessProbe**: `exec` running `["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"]`, `periodSeconds=15`.
- **readinessProbe**: `httpGet` path `/` port `80`, `initialDelaySeconds=5`.
- **startupProbe**: `tcpSocket` port `80`, `failureThreshold=30`, `periodSeconds=10`.
questions.hint: All three go under the same container. Use `exec.command` for liveness, `httpGet` for readiness, `tcpSocket` for startup — mind the exact timing fields.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: health-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    livenessProbe:
      exec: { command: ["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"] }
      periodSeconds: 15
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    startupProbe:
      tcpSocket: { port: 80 }
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
YAML
questions.eli5:
Kubernetes can't *see* inside your app, so it keeps poking it to ask "you good?" These pokes are **probes**, and there are three kinds that answer three different questions:

- **livenessProbe** — "Are you still alive, or did you freeze?" If it fails, Kubernetes **restarts** the container. Think: a nurse checking a pulse; no pulse → call the crash team.
- **readinessProbe** — "Are you ready to take customers right now?" If it fails, Kubernetes stops sending traffic (**pulls it out of the Service**) but doesn't restart it. Think: a shop flipping its "Open/Back in 5 min" sign.
- **startupProbe** — "Have you finished booting up yet?" For slow starters. While it's still checking, the other two probes are **paused** so a slow boot isn't mistaken for a crash. Think: giving a sleepy engine extra time to warm up before the dashboard warning lights are allowed to trip.

Each poke can be done three ways (**handlers**): run a command inside the container (`exec`), make an HTTP request (`httpGet`), or just knock on a TCP port (`tcpSocket`).

**Watch out for:**

- **Timing fields attach per-probe.** `periodSeconds`, `initialDelaySeconds`, `failureThreshold` each go on the specific probe you mean — don't put them in the wrong block.
- **liveness restarts; readiness only removes traffic; startup gates the other two.** Mixing these up is the classic mistake.
- **A too-aggressive liveness probe causes restart loops** — if the app is just slow to start, use a startupProbe instead of a short liveness delay.
- **`httpGet` needs a `path` and `port`; `tcpSocket` needs a `port`; `exec` needs a `command`.** One handler per probe.
- **While the startupProbe is still running, liveness/readiness don't fire at all** — that's the whole point of it.
questions.deepDive:
## Probes — three kinds, three handlers

### Mental model
Probes are the kubelet periodically checking a container's health. **Three kinds** answer different questions and take different actions; **three handlers** are the ways to check. Timing fields attach **per-probe**.

| Probe | Question | On failure |
|---|---|---|
| `livenessProbe` | still alive? | **restart** the container |
| `readinessProbe` | ready for traffic? | remove Pod from **Service endpoints** (no restart) |
| `startupProbe` | finished starting? | restart if it never passes; **disables liveness/readiness until it succeeds** |

### The three handlers
| Handler | Checks | Required fields |
|---|---|---|
| `exec` | command exit code 0 = pass | `command: [...]` |
| `httpGet` | HTTP status 200–399 = pass | `path`, `port` (+ `httpHeaders`, `scheme`) |
| `tcpSocket` | TCP connect succeeds | `port` |

(There's also `grpc` with a `port` on modern clusters.)

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    livenessProbe:
      exec: { command: ["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"] }
      periodSeconds: 15
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    startupProbe:
      tcpSocket: { port: 80 }
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
```

### Timing fields (per-probe)
| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `initialDelaySeconds` | 0 | wait before the first check |
| `periodSeconds` | 10 | interval between checks |
| `timeoutSeconds` | 1 | per-check timeout |
| `failureThreshold` | 3 | consecutive failures → fail the probe |
| `successThreshold` | 1 | consecutive successes → pass (must be 1 for liveness/startup) |

**Startup budget** = `failureThreshold × periodSeconds`. Here `30 × 10s = 300s` for the app to come up before being killed.

### How startupProbe interacts
- While the startupProbe has not yet succeeded, **liveness and readiness probes do not run**.
- Once it passes **once**, it stops and liveness/readiness take over.
- This is the correct tool for slow-starting apps — far better than a huge `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe.

### liveness vs readiness — don't confuse the action
- **Liveness failing** → kubelet kills & restarts the container (can cause crash loops if misconfigured).
- **Readiness failing** → Pod's IP is removed from all its Services' Endpoints; the container keeps running and can recover.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod health-pod
kubectl -n pod-design describe pod health-pod | grep -A2 -iE 'Liveness|Readiness|Startup'
kubectl -n pod-design get pod health-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].livenessProbe.periodSeconds}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Each timing field goes on its own probe** — a `periodSeconds` meant for liveness won't help readiness.
- **Wrong probe choice**: using liveness where readiness is needed causes restarts instead of traffic removal (and vice-versa).
- **Aggressive liveness = restart loops.** For slow boots, add a `startupProbe`, not a tiny liveness delay.
- **`successThreshold` must be 1** for liveness and startup probes (only readiness may be >1).
- **`httpGet.port`** may be a number or a named container port; **exec** runs *inside* the container (needs the binary present).
- **Default `timeoutSeconds` is 1** — slow endpoints may spuriously fail; bump it when needed.
- Probes also apply to native sidecars; classic init containers don't get probes.

### Quick reference
```yaml
livenessProbe:  { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"] }, periodSeconds: 15 }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }, initialDelaySeconds: 5 }
startupProbe:   { tcpSocket: { port: 80 }, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 10 }
```

questions.title: Lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown
questions.teach:
**Lifecycle hooks** on a container run code around its life: `lifecycle.postStart` fires right after the container starts, `lifecycle.preStop` fires before SIGTERM on shutdown. `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (on the pod `spec`) is how long preStop + SIGTERM get before SIGKILL.

**Gotcha:** a `preStop` that runs longer than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is cut off by SIGKILL.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `graceful-pod` in `pod-design` (`nginx:1.25`, container `web`) with:
- `lifecycle.postStart` exec `["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"]`
- `lifecycle.preStop` exec `["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"]`
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`
questions.hint: `lifecycle.postStart.exec.command` and `lifecycle.preStop.exec.command` live on the container; `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` lives on the pod `spec`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: graceful-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    lifecycle:
      postStart: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"] } }
      preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"] } }
YAML

verification.description: graceful-pod: postStart + preStop exec hooks + terminationGracePeriodSeconds 30

questions.eli5:
Every container has a birth and a death, and **lifecycle hooks** let you run a little script at each moment — like leaving a note that says "do this the instant you wake up" and another that says "do this right before you go to sleep."

- **postStart** runs **right after** the container starts. Here it scribbles "started" into a file — handy for warming caches, registering, or signaling "I'm up."
- **preStop** runs **right before** Kubernetes sends the shutdown signal (SIGTERM). Here it tells nginx to "finish serving what you're serving, then quit cleanly" (`nginx -s quit`) — this is **graceful shutdown**: letting in-flight requests finish instead of yanking the plug.

Now, Kubernetes isn't infinitely patient. **terminationGracePeriodSeconds** is a countdown timer (here, 30 seconds) that starts at shutdown. Within that window, preStop runs and the app gets its polite SIGTERM to wrap up. If the timer hits zero and the container still hasn't exited, Kubernetes stops being polite and sends SIGKILL — the instant, non-negotiable "you're done" signal.

**Watch out for:**

- **A preStop that runs longer than the grace period gets cut off** by SIGKILL. Make sure 30s is enough for your cleanup, or raise the number.
- **`postStart`/`preStop` live on the container** (under `lifecycle`); **`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` lives on the pod `spec`.** Different levels.
- **The grace-period clock covers preStop AND SIGTERM together** — they don't each get a fresh 30s.
- **postStart has no ordering guarantee with the entrypoint** — it may run before the main process is fully up, and if it fails the container is killed.
- **Hooks use the same handlers as probes** (`exec`, `httpGet`) — here it's `exec`.
questions.deepDive:
## Lifecycle hooks & graceful shutdown

### Mental model
**Lifecycle hooks** run code at two moments of a container's life: `postStart` (just after start) and `preStop` (just before SIGTERM). `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (pod-level) is the total budget for an orderly shutdown — `preStop` **plus** SIGTERM must finish within it, or the kubelet sends **SIGKILL**.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30          # POD level
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    lifecycle:                               # CONTAINER level
      postStart:
        exec: { command: ["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"] }
      preStop:
        exec: { command: ["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"] }
```

### The termination sequence
```
1. Pod marked Terminating; removed from Service endpoints
2. preStop hook runs (if any)           ┐
3. SIGTERM sent to PID 1 of container   │  all within
4. App does graceful shutdown           │  terminationGracePeriodSeconds
5. If still alive at deadline → SIGKILL  ┘
```
The grace-period clock starts when termination begins and covers **steps 2–4 together** (preStop does **not** get its own separate budget on top of SIGTERM).

### Hooks
| Hook | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `postStart` | immediately after container create | runs **async** with the entrypoint — no ordering guarantee; if it fails, the container is killed |
| `preStop` | before SIGTERM, on termination | blocking — SIGTERM waits for it (within the grace period) |

Handlers: `exec`, `httpGet`, `tcpSocket` (same set as probes); `sleep` is also available on newer clusters.

### Field placement
| Field | Level |
|---|---|
| `lifecycle.postStart` / `lifecycle.preStop` | **container** |
| `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` | **pod spec** |

### Graceful shutdown patterns
- **`nginx -s quit`** — finish in-flight requests, then exit (vs `-s stop` which is immediate).
- **preStop `sleep`** — give load balancers time to deregister the endpoint before the process stops, avoiding dropped connections.
- Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` ≥ (preStop time + app drain time).

### Override grace period on delete
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design delete pod graceful-pod --grace-period=10   # force a shorter window
kubectl -n pod-design delete pod graceful-pod --grace-period=0 --force   # immediate SIGKILL
```

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod graceful-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}'; echo   # 30
kubectl -n pod-design exec graceful-pod -- cat /tmp/poststart                                          # started
kubectl -n pod-design describe pod graceful-pod | grep -iE 'PostStart|PreStop|Grace'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **preStop longer than the grace period is truncated by SIGKILL** — size `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` accordingly.
- **Hooks are container-level; grace period is pod-level** — classic placement trap.
- **One shared budget** covers preStop + SIGTERM, not one each.
- **postStart isn't ordered vs the entrypoint** and a failing postStart kills the container — keep it fast and safe.
- **SIGTERM goes to PID 1** — your app (or an init-process wrapper) must actually handle it, or it'll be SIGKILLed at the deadline.
- Hooks fire at least once but may run more than once on edge cases — make them idempotent.

### Quick reference
```yaml
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
lifecycle:
  postStart: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"] } }
  preStop:   { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"] } }
```
